title: Krishna takes the reins
hook: Arjuna chooses Krishna, unarmed, over a whole army, and asks him to drive
carry: bhakti: choosing god over the army
tomorrow: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born

segments.voice: Yesterday: the eve, and Arjuna's bow slipping from his hand. The Gita begins with Arjuna's despair.

Before the war, before the conches, there's a scene the Mahabharata tells almost like a joke. Arjuna and Duryodhana both go to Krishna to ask for his help in the coming war. Krishna is asleep. Duryodhana arrives first and sits proudly by his head. Arjuna comes in and sits quietly at his feet. Krishna wakes, and the first person he sees is Arjuna. So he makes an offer. On one side, my whole army, a vast force of warriors. On the other, me, alone, and I won't lift a weapon in the war. Choose.
screen: `TWO COUSINS AT KRISHNA'S BED.` → `ONE AT HIS HEAD, ONE AT HIS FEET.` → `MY ARMY, OR ME, UNARMED.`

segments.voice: Arjuna, asked first, chooses Krishna. No army, just him, unarmed. Duryodhana can hardly believe his luck: he gets the army. Then Arjuna asks Krishna for one thing: drive my chariot. So the one the Gita will reveal as God becomes a driver, a sarathi, the one who holds the reins. Look at the choice. Duryodhana counted soldiers. Arjuna chose the presence of God, even a God who promised not to fight. Many devotees read this choice as the heart of bhakti, loving devotion, one of Hinduism's great paths: what matters most isn't how much power is on your side, but whether God is with you. Krishna is still called Parthasarathi, the charioteer of Arjuna, and there are temples to him by that name. You'll see the picture on home altars and on the covers of the Gita: Krishna holding the reins, Arjuna listening. For many devotees it's a prayer without words: you drive. And that's where this long run of stories pauses. A boy made of earth at a door. A leap across the sea. Sandals on a throne. A row of lamps. Cousins, dice, a cloth that wouldn't end, five villages, and a frightened man in a chariot. When someone mentions Hanuman now, or Draupadi, or Bharata's sandals, you won't nod politely. You'll know them, and what they teach. Next come the practices these stories were pointing at all along. And when a festival's date arrives, its story comes first.
screen: `ARJUNA CHOOSES KRISHNA: DRIVE MY CHARIOT.` · `BHAKTI: CHOOSING GOD OVER THE ARMY.` · `PARTHASARATHI, ON HOME ALTARS.` · `YOU KNOW THESE PEOPLE NOW.`

segments.voice: Picture a chariot, and Krishna holding the reins. Then picture something in your life that feels like a battlefield right now. Ask honestly: am I counting soldiers, or asking who's with me? If you pray, offer the reins: say, in your own words, you drive. If you don't, name what steadies you when your hands shake. Then let a few faces walk past: Ganesha, Hanuman, Sita, Draupadi, Arjuna. Notice which one stops and looks at you.
The driver. Sarathi, the one who holds the reins: Krishna, choosing to drive Arjuna's chariot instead of fighting.
Your line: bhakti, choosing God over the army. Arjuna chose Krishna, and asked him to drive. See you tomorrow.
